title: Event-Driven Order Processing System
question: Design an event-driven order processing system using Kafka. Requirements: 1) Order placement triggers cascade of events (OrderCreated, PaymentProcessed, InventoryReserved, ShippingScheduled), 2) Each service consumes relevant events and publishes new events, 3) Handle failures gracefully with compensation events (PaymentFailed → CancelOrder), 4) Maintain event ordering per order (use order_id as partition key), 5) Support event replay for debugging and recovery, 6) Implement event versioning for schema evolution, 7) Provide event audit trail for compliance. Discuss: implementing event choreography where OrderService publishes OrderCreated event to order-events topic, PaymentService consumes OrderCreated and publishes PaymentProcessed/PaymentFailed, using order_id as partition key to ensure ordered processing per order, storing events in event store (database table or Kafka compacted topic) for replay, implementing event versioning with schema registry (Avro/Protobuf) for backward/forward compatibility, handling compensating events (if InventoryService fails, publish InventoryReservationFailed → PaymentService refunds → OrderService cancels order), implementing dead letter topic for failed events, using Kafka transactions for exactly-once event processing, implementing event sourcing to reconstruct order state from events, creating read models (order status view) from event stream, monitoring event lag per consumer, and implementing correlation IDs for tracing events across services.

title: Scalable Multi-Channel Notification System
question: Design a notification system supporting email, SMS, and push notifications at scale. Requirements: 1) Handle 1 million notifications per hour, 2) Support different priority levels (high, medium, low), 3) Implement retry with exponential backoff for failures, 4) Prevent duplicate notifications, 5) Support notification templating and personalization, 6) Track delivery status (sent, delivered, failed, bounced), 7) Support batch notifications and scheduled notifications. Discuss: using RabbitMQ with priority queues for notification distribution (high priority queue processed first), creating separate workers for each channel (EmailWorker, SMSWorker, PushWorker) consuming from channel-specific queues, implementing idempotency using unique notification_id stored in Redis (check before sending, prevent duplicates), using message TTL for time-sensitive notifications, implementing retry mechanism with exponential backoff using RabbitMQ delayed message plugin or dead letter exchange with TTL, storing notification templates in database with placeholder variables, enriching templates with user data before sending, tracking delivery in notification_log table with status updates, using Kafka for notification events (NotificationSent, NotificationDelivered) for analytics, implementing rate limiting per channel (SMTP rate limits, SMS quotas), batching notifications to same user within time window, scheduling notifications using scheduled executor + database (fetch due notifications and publish to queue), monitoring queue depth and consumer lag, and handling provider failures with circuit breaker pattern.

title: Distributed Audit Log with Kafka
question: Design an audit logging system capturing all changes across microservices. Requirements: 1) Log every state-changing operation (CREATE, UPDATE, DELETE) from all services, 2) Capture who, what, when, where, why for each change, 3) Ensure audit logs are immutable and tamper-proof, 4) Support querying audit logs by entity, user, date range, action, 5) Retain audit data for 7 years (compliance), 6) Handle high write volume (10K audit events/second), 7) Provide real-time alerting on suspicious activities. Discuss: each microservice publishes AuditEvent to Kafka audit-log topic after every state change, event contains user_id, action, resource_type, resource_id, timestamp, before/after values, IP address, creating Kafka consumer that persists events to time-series database (TimescaleDB) or data warehouse (S3 + Athena) for long-term storage and querying, partitioning audit-log topic by service or date for parallelism, using Kafka's log compaction + infinite retention for immutable audit trail (or separate cold storage), implementing append-only audit table with no UPDATE/DELETE permissions to ensure immutability, creating indexes on user_id, resource_id, timestamp, action for fast queries, using Kafka Streams for real-time pattern detection (multiple failed login attempts, privilege escalation), aggregating audit events into rollup tables for reporting, implementing GDPR-compliant data redaction (encrypt PII fields, support right to erasure with tombstone events), monitoring audit pipeline lag, and archiving old audit data to S3 with partitioning by year/month for cost efficiency.

title: Change Data Capture for Data Replication
question: Implement Change Data Capture (CDC) to replicate data from transactional database to analytics database. Requirements: 1) Capture all INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE operations from PostgreSQL, 2) Stream changes to Kafka in real-time, 3) Apply changes to analytics database (Elasticsearch) for search, data warehouse (BigQuery) for reporting, 4) Maintain data consistency between source and targets, 5) Support initial snapshot load + continuous incremental updates, 6) Handle schema changes gracefully, 7) Minimize impact on source database performance. Discuss: using Debezium connector for PostgreSQL CDC (reads transaction log/WAL), publishing change events to Kafka topics (one per table, e.g., db.users, db.orders), event contains operation type (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), before/after values, timestamp, transaction ID, creating Kafka consumers (ElasticsearchSink, BigQuerySink) that apply changes to target systems, using Kafka Connect for managed sink connectors, implementing initial snapshot by reading entire table and publishing to Kafka, switching to incremental CDC after snapshot complete, handling schema evolution with Schema Registry (Avro schema includes field types, supports backward/forward compatibility), transforming data in stream (Kafka Streams or KSQL) before loading to targets (filter sensitive fields, aggregate data), ensuring exactly-once delivery with Kafka transactions and idempotent consumers (use primary key for upsert), monitoring replication lag (compare source DB timestamp with applied timestamp), handling large transactions (split into smaller batches), and minimal source DB impact (Debezium reads logs, no query overhead).

title: Saga Pattern with Messaging Orchestration
question: Implement orchestration-based Saga pattern using messaging for distributed transactions. Requirements: 1) Coordinate multi-step workflow (create order, charge payment, reserve inventory, schedule shipping), 2) Central orchestrator manages saga state and invokes services, 3) Each service publishes command responses (Success/Failure) to reply queues, 4) Orchestrator listens to responses and decides next step or triggers compensation, 5) Support long-running sagas (may take minutes/hours), 6) Persist saga state for recovery after crashes, 7) Provide saga visualization for monitoring. Discuss: creating OrderSagaOrchestrator service that manages saga state machine, storing saga state in database (saga_id, current_step, status, data, created_at), orchestrator publishes commands to service-specific queues (payment-commands, inventory-commands), services process commands and publish responses to saga-responses queue with correlation_id (saga_id), orchestrator consumes responses and transitions saga state (Payment Success → Reserve Inventory), implementing compensation logic (if inventory fails, orchestrator publishes CancelPayment command), using RabbitMQ request-reply pattern with reply-to queue, handling timeouts (if service doesn't respond in 30s, trigger compensation), persisting each state transition for crash recovery (on restart, load incomplete sagas and resume), implementing saga compensation in reverse order (last successful step compensated first), visualizing saga state in admin UI (show saga flowchart with completed/pending/failed steps), using Spring State Machine for orchestrator logic, monitoring saga completion time and failure rates, and handling concurrent saga updates with optimistic locking (version field in saga table).

title: Advanced Retry and Dead Letter Handling
question: Design sophisticated retry mechanism with dead letter queue handling. Requirements: 1) Retry transient failures (network timeout, rate limit) with exponential backoff, 2) Permanent failures (invalid data, business rule violation) go directly to DLQ, 3) Support configurable retry limits (max 5 retries), 4) Track retry count and history per message, 5) Provide DLQ monitoring and reprocessing capability, 6) Alert on DLQ threshold (> 100 messages), 7) Analyze DLQ messages to identify patterns. Discuss: implementing Spring Kafka error handler with RetryTemplate for automatic retries, distinguishing between retriable (IOException, TimeoutException) and non-retriable (IllegalArgumentException, ValidationException) exceptions using custom logic, using exponential backoff strategy (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s), adding retry_count header to message on each retry, publishing to DLT (dead-letter-topic) after max retries exhausted or non-retriable exception, storing DLQ messages in database for analysis (message_id, payload, error, retry_history, timestamp), creating DLQ monitoring dashboard showing message count, error types, trends, implementing reprocessing mechanism (admin marks message as ready for retry → republished to original topic), alerting via Slack/PagerDuty when DLQ depth exceeds threshold, using Kafka Streams to analyze DLQ patterns (group by error type, find most common failures), implementing poison pill handling (if same message fails repeatedly, mark as permanently failed and skip), using separate DLQ per error category (transient-dlq, validation-dlq, system-dlq) for targeted handling, and periodic DLQ cleanup job (archive messages older than 90 days).

title: Event Sourcing with CQRS and Kafka
question: Implement Event Sourcing and CQRS using Kafka as event store. Requirements: 1) All state changes stored as immutable events in Kafka, 2) Current state derived by replaying events, 3) Separate command and query models, 4) Support temporal queries (state at specific point in time), 5) Handle high event volume (100K events/second), 6) Support multiple read models optimized for different queries, 7) Ensure consistency between event store and read models. Discuss: using Kafka as event store with one topic per aggregate (account-events, order-events), each event has aggregate_id as partition key for ordering, commands (DepositMoney, WithdrawMoney) generate events (MoneyDeposited, MoneyWithdrawn) published to Kafka, implementing event versioning with Schema Registry, creating projection services that consume events and build read models (account-balance table, transaction-history table, monthly-summary materialized view), using Kafka Streams for projections with state stores for local caching, ensuring eventual consistency (read models lag behind write model by seconds), implementing snapshots for performance (store aggregate state every 100 events, replay only recent events), supporting temporal queries by replaying events up to specific timestamp (create temporary projection), using KSQL for ad-hoc querying of event stream, handling event replay for rebuilding projections (consume from beginning, clear old data, rebuild), implementing optimistic concurrency control with event version number, monitoring projection lag (compare event timestamp with projection timestamp), and scaling horizontally by adding more projection instances (Kafka consumer groups).

title: Guaranteed Message Ordering Across Services
question: Ensure message ordering in distributed system with multiple consumers. Requirements: 1) Messages for same entity must be processed in order (all operations on Order #123 processed sequentially), 2) Support parallel processing of messages for different entities, 3) Handle consumer failures without breaking ordering, 4) Scale consumers horizontally while maintaining ordering, 5) Minimize latency impact of ordering constraint, 6) Support reprocessing failed messages without disorder. Discuss: using partition key strategy in Kafka (set order_id as key, Kafka guarantees order within partition), each partition assigned to single consumer in consumer group (ordering guaranteed), scaling by increasing partitions (not consumers, since more consumers than partitions breaks ordering), implementing idempotent processing to handle duplicate messages during reprocessing, using sticky partition assignment strategy to minimize rebalancing, handling consumer failure with pause/resume (stop processing messages for affected partitions until issue resolved), implementing sequential processing within consumer (process one message at a time per partition, no async), using manual offset commit only after successful processing (auto-commit can break ordering on failure), implementing version/sequence number in messages to detect and handle out-of-order messages, using global ordering with single partition (extreme case, limits throughput), alternative: application-level locking (acquire distributed lock on entity_id before processing, ensures order across partitions), monitoring message lag per partition, and trade-offs between strict ordering (lower throughput) vs eventual consistency (higher throughput).

title: Multi-Datacenter Kafka Replication
question: Design Kafka setup spanning multiple datacenters for disaster recovery and low latency. Requirements: 1) Active-active setup where both DCs handle writes, 2) Replicate messages between DCs for redundancy, 3) Minimize cross-DC latency impact on producers, 4) Handle network partitions between DCs gracefully, 5) Support failover to backup DC if primary fails, 6) Avoid message duplication in cross-DC replication, 7) Ensure compliance with data residency (certain data stays in specific DC). Discuss: using MirrorMaker 2 for cross-DC replication (mirrors topics from DC1 to DC2 and vice versa), configuring producers to publish to local Kafka cluster (low latency), consumers in each DC can read from local cluster or remote cluster based on requirement, implementing data classification (global topics replicated across DCs, regional topics stay local for compliance), handling conflicts in active-active (use conflict resolution strategy: last-write-wins based on timestamp, or application-specific merge logic), configuring MirrorMaker with offset translation for consumer failover (map DC1 offsets to DC2 offsets), implementing disaster recovery plan (if DC1 fails, redirect producers to DC2, consumers continue from last checkpoint), using Kafka stretched cluster (single cluster spanning DCs with rack-awareness, but high latency risk), implementing geo-fencing for data residency (EU data stays in EU DC, route based on user location), monitoring replication lag between DCs (alert if lag exceeds threshold), handling network partition with circuit breaker (stop replication if unreachable, resume when network restored), and trade-offs between consistency (synchronous replication, high latency) vs availability (asynchronous replication, potential data loss).

title: Exactly-Once Message Processing Guarantee
question: Implement exactly-once processing semantics to prevent duplicate operations. Requirements: 1) Ensure each message processed exactly once despite retries, 2) Handle producer retries without creating duplicate messages, 3) Support idempotent operations in consumer, 4) Coordinate message processing with database transactions, 5) Handle failures and crashes without data loss or duplication, 6) Minimize performance impact of exactly-once semantics. Discuss: enabling Kafka producer idempotence (enable.idempotence=true, producer automatically deduplicates retries), using Kafka transactions for atomic writes (begin transaction, produce messages, commit), implementing transactional consumers (read committed isolation level, only see committed messages), coordinating Kafka consumption with database transaction using transaction outbox pattern (consume message + write to DB + commit offset in single transaction), implementing idempotency key in consumer (generate unique ID from message content, store in idempotency_keys table, skip if already processed), using at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing (safe to process twice, no side effects), storing processed message IDs in Redis with TTL (fast duplicate check), handling exactly-once end-to-end (producer → Kafka → consumer → database all transactional), understanding performance trade-off (transactions add latency ~10-20ms), using Kafka's transactional ID for producer (ensures single writer per partition), implementing two-phase commit for cross-system consistency (Kafka + database), and monitoring transaction abort rates and duplicate detection rates.
